title: Partner apps must enable bulk operations before use
summary:
Starting today, apps need access to bulk operations before they can run bulk queries or bulk mutations with the GraphQL Admin API. You can enable access for your app in the Partner Dashboard.

What changed

Bulk queries and bulk mutations are enabled separately:

  • To run bulkOperationRunQuery, your app needs access to bulk queries.
  • To run bulkOperationRunMutation, your app needs access to bulk mutations.

If your app starts a bulk operation without access, then the request returns an access denied error. The requirement applies to all GraphQL Admin API versions.

Who's affected

Public apps and custom apps that you build as a partner and that run bulk operations. Apps that merchants create in the Shopify admin or the Dev Dashboard aren't affected at this time.

If your app already runs bulk operations, then we've already enabled access for it. You can confirm this in the Partner Dashboard.

Apps that haven't run a bulk query or bulk mutation in the last 31 days lose access to that operation type. If your app loses access, then follow the steps below to enable it again.

What to do

Check your app's access and enable the operation types that it runs:

  1. From the Partner Dashboard, go to Apps, and then select your app.
  2. In the sidebar, click API access requests.
  3. Under Run bulk operations, click Allow bulk queries, Allow bulk mutations, or both. If an operation type is already enabled, then the section shows that it's enabled.

You don't need to change your app configuration, release a new app version, or ask merchants to reinstall your app. Access applies to every store that has your app installed.

For details, see Enabling access to bulk operations.

title: Merchant notes on store credit transactions
summary:
As of GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01, you can attach a merchant-only note when crediting or debiting a store credit account and read those notes on store credit transactions. Notes are optional, so existing integrations continue to work without changes or required updates.

What changed

  • StoreCreditAccountCreditInput and StoreCreditAccountDebitInput accept an optional note string.
  • StoreCreditAccountTransaction.note returns the stored note for credit, debit, and debit-revert transactions, or null when no note is set. Expiration transactions always return null.
  • Notes support up to 5,000 characters. Longer notes return a NOTE_TOO_LONG user error and the API doesn’t create the transaction.
  • Notes are for merchants only and aren't visible to customers. You can set a note when you create a transaction, but you can’t edit a note on an existing transaction.

Who's affected

This change applies to apps that manage store credit using GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01 or later. Versions 2026-10 and earlier don’t expose these fields.

Existing read_store_credit_account_transactions and write_store_credit_account_transactions access scopes and permission requirements still apply. No new scope is required.

What to do

You don’t need to change existing integrations. To start using notes:

  1. Target GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01 or later in your app.
  2. When you create a credit or debit, include note in the input.
  3. Select note on the returned StoreCreditAccountTransaction to read the stored value.
  4. Test in a dev store by creating a transaction with a note and verifying that the response includes the expected note string.

Related docs

  • storeCreditAccountCredit mutation reference
  • storeCreditAccountDebit mutation reference

title: App security updates: IP allowlist is now required
summary:
On Oct 27 we recommended the IP allowlist. It is now required for every public app by November 20, or November 12 if you use bulk ops. An IP allowlist means a leaked token can't be used anywhere but your own servers. With the busiest weeks of the year for merchants almost here, we're asking for it now.

Action required

  • All public apps that call the Admin API: Turn on the IP allowlist by November 20, 2026 at 11:59 PM ET. With it on, your tokens only work from the addresses or networks you list, so a leaked token can't be used anywhere else. The IP allowlist is required for public apps. If you're on serverless or dynamic IPs, you'll need to allowlist by network with ASN support instead.

  • Bulk operations: Turn on the IP allowlist by November 12, 2026 at 11:59 PM ET. After that date, bulk queries and mutations from public apps without an IP allowlist are blocked.

Also this week

  • Merchants can now see your app's security setup in Settings > Apps: expiring tokens and IP allowlist. After November 20, apps without an IP allowlist are flagged.
  • Find non-expiring tokens fast: filter your Dev Dashboard API logs by token type. And our Token Expiry FAQ answers the most common questions.
  • Network access testing in dev store previews: You can now test your network_access declarations before you release. It flags any site or server your app uses that you haven't declared yet. Test network access in dev store previews
  • Run app security checks in CI/CD. A new tutorial walks you through how to automatically scan your app for security issues.
  • Coming soon, access scopes for bulk operations: Bulk queries and bulk mutations will each need their own scope. If your app ran a bulk operation in the last 180 days, Shopify grants the scopes automatically. Once they're live, add them to your app config before your next deploy. We'll share the changelog with the scope names when ready.

If you miss a deadline

To protect merchant security, we'll begin enforcing IP allowlists starting in November. The timelines for expiring offline access tokens remain the same. In both cases, existing installs keep working until April 1, 2027:

| | IP allowlist | Expiring offline access tokens | | :

title: IP allowlists are now required for public apps
summary:
We're enhancing protection of merchants by adding IP allowlist configuration as a requirement for public apps. All public apps using bulk operations must configure an allowlist by November 12, 2026, and all other public apps must configure an allowlist by November 20, 2026.

If an app is not migrated by these dates:

  • November 12, 2026 at 11:59 PM ET.: Bulk operations from public apps without an IP allowlist will fail to execute.
  • November 20, 2026 at 11:59 PM ET: Public apps without an IP allowlist will be delisted from the Shopify App Store and blocked from new installs.

What apps are affected

All public apps.

What apps are unaffected

  • Custom apps
  • Apps created by merchants either in the Dev Dashboard or in the admin

Why we're making this change

Leaked tokens can be used from any network location. IP allowlists reduce the impact of a credential leak by limiting the networks from which your app can invoke the Admin API.

What to do

Configure your app's allowed IPs in the Dev Dashboard:

  • If your app calls Shopify from static IP addresses, configure your IP allowlist based on static IPs or CIDR range.
  • If your app's egress IP addresses are dynamic, allow your hosting provider's ASNs and list the countries your app runs in.

For setup instructions, see Restrict API access with an IP allowlist.

What if my app makes Admin API calls from merchant infrastructure?

You should move as quickly as possible to an architecture that better limits exposure of Admin API tokens. You may submit a request for an extension to the deadlines above.

title: App IP allowlists now support apps with serverless hosting through ASNs
summary:
Apps without static IP addresses, such as apps on serverless platforms, can now add your hosting provider's autonomous system numbers (ASNs) to your app's IP allowlist in the Dev Dashboard.

What changed

The IP allowlist section of your app's Settings page now lets you allow either IP addresses or Networks (ASN). For networks, enter up to 10 ASNs and limit them to up to 10 countries. Test them against recent traffic, then turn on enforcement. Requests from outside your allowed networks fail with a 403 status code.

What to do

IP allowlists will soon be required for all public apps. Shopify strongly recommends all apps use an IP allowlist.

If your app calls Shopify from static IP addresses, keep allowing those addresses. If your app's egress IP addresses are dynamic, allow your hosting provider's ASNs and list the countries your app runs in.

For setup instructions, see Restrict API access with an IP allowlist.

title: Test app network access configuration on dev stores
summary:
You can now test your app's [network_access] settings on a dev store with the new network access testing feature preview. The preview helps you confirm you have the right networks listed, and find hosts and servers you missed.

What changed

When you create a dev store with the network_access_testing feature preview, you can confirm your network configuration behaves as expected:

  • Links to hosts that aren't in allowed_navigation_hosts show the exit warning, so you can ensure you're warning when appropriate and not showing exit warnings for trusted hosts.
  • The browser console warns when a storefront page loads from or sends requests to a server that isn't in allowed_sources. The preview only warns. It doesn't block anything.

Who's affected

Any app whose code links to or contacts external servers from a storefront can use this new testing option. Shopify recommends all apps configure these settings to avoid navigation warnings on merchant sites, and to help Shopify spot suspicious activity.

What to do

For step-by-step instructions and troubleshooting, follow the steps to test network access configuration on a dev store.

title: RETRY_DECLINED added to CustomerPaymentMethodRevocationReason
summary:
As of GraphQL Admin API version2027-01, CustomerPaymentMethod.revokedReason can return a new value: RETRY_DECLINED. Shopify uses this value when a subscription payment method is revoked because the payment processor has blocked any further retry attempts. On earlier API versions, these revocations continue to return TOO_MANY_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURES.

If your app reads CustomerPaymentMethod.revokedReason using API version 2027-01, use RETRY_DECLINED to indicate to merchants and buyers that the processor has blocked further charges to the saved payment method and that a different payment method is required.

The customer_payment_methods/revoke webhook payload is unchanged. After receiving the webhook, query CustomerPaymentMethod.revokedReason to determine whether the payment method was revoked because of RETRY_DECLINED or TOO_MANY_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURES.

title: currententrychange now returns the previous page in event.from for customer account full-page extensions
summary:
Starting in API version 2027-01, in customer account full-page extensions the Navigation API currententrychange event sets event.from to the page the customer navigated away from, instead of the page they navigated to. This is a breaking change for customer account full-page extensions that read the new page from event.from. Update them to read shopify.navigation.currentEntry before you move them to 2027-01.

What changed

In customer account full-page extensions (customer-account.page.render and customer-account.order.page.render), currententrychange passes a NavigationCurrentEntryChangeEvent whose from property is documented as the previous history entry. In API version 2026-10 and earlier, from is the new entry instead, the same value as shopify.navigation.currentEntry. Starting in 2027-01, from is the previous entry.

Who's affected

Full-page extensions on API version 2027-01 or later that use event.from to find the page the customer navigated to are affected.

Extensions on 2026-10 and earlier aren't affected, because their behavior doesn't change. Extensions that read shopify.navigation.currentEntry, including extensions that use the useNavigationCurrentEntry hook, aren't affected on any version.

Breaking changes and migrations

On 2027-01, code that reads the new page from event.from.url gets the previous page's URL instead. For example, an extension that chooses which route to render from event.from keeps showing the previous route after each navigation.

Replace those reads with shopify.navigation.currentEntry.url.

Before:

shopify.navigation.addEventListener('currententrychange', (event) => {
  setPath(new URL(event.from.url).pathname);
});

After:

shopify.navigation.addEventListener('currententrychange', () => {
  setPath(new URL(shopify.navigation.currentEntry.url).pathname);
});

The updated code works on API version 2025-10 and later, so you can make the change before you update your API version.

Action required

Before you update a customer account full-page extension to 2027-01, update every currententrychange handler that reads the new page from event.from. To confirm the update, navigate between two routes in your extension and check that each navigation shows the page you navigated to.

Related docs

  • Navigation API reference for customer account UI extensions

title: UI extensions now support a larger number of locales
summary:
UI extensions no longer have a 256 KB limit on the combined size of their locale files. As of October 30, 2026, you can add more languages to an extension without hitting a combined size limit at deploy. This applies to all apps with UI extensions, and no action is required.

What changed

Previously, the total size of the locale files in a UI extension's locales folder couldn't exceed 256 KB. Extensions with many languages could reach that limit and fail to deploy, which forced you to trim translations or drop languages.

That combined limit is now removed. The 30 KB limit for each individual locale file still applies. Locale files keep the same format, file naming, and fallback behavior described in the checkout UI extension localization guide. You don't need to change how you structure translations.

Who's affected

This change applies to every app that includes UI extensions with locale files, on all API versions. Existing extension versions keep working as before. New deploys aren't limited by the combined size of locale files.

If your extensions were under the old limit, nothing changes for you.

What to do

You don't need to take any action. If you previously removed languages or shortened translations to stay under 256 KB, you can add them back:

  1. Add the locale files you need to your extension's locales folder, for example de.json or pt-BR.json. Keep each file under 30 KB.
  2. Run shopify app deploy to release a new app version.
  3. Preview the extension in a development store with the store or customer locale set to one of the new languages, and confirm the translated strings appear.

Related docs

  • Localize a checkout UI extension
  • Localize a customer account UI extension

title: Gift Card line_item_id will become read-only in REST Admin API version 2027-01
summary:
In REST Admin API version 2027-01 and later, the line_item_id property on the Gift Card resource is read-only. Shopify ignores the property in create and update requests. Remove it from those requests before you upgrade.

What changed

In REST Admin API version 2027-01 and later, apps can't add, replace, or clear a gift card's line-item association through Gift Card create or update requests. Shopify ignores any line_item_id value in those requests.

Gift Card responses still include existing line-item and order associations. Earlier API versions keep their current behavior.

Who's affected

This change affects you if all of the following are true:

  • Your app uses the REST Admin API Gift Card resource.
  • Your app includes line_item_id when it creates or updates gift cards.

title: New trusted vault origin signal in Payments Apps API
summary:
The Payments Apps API 2027-01 release candidate adds payment_method.data.trusted_vault_origin to credit card payment and verification requests. Payment app developers can use this optional Boolean to handle missing CVV for cards from a vault Shopify trusts. Adoption is optional and requires Shopify enablement.

What changed

Shopify can include trusted_vault_origin in both encrypted card and payment_instrument payloads. Read it from payment_method.data, outside the encrypted card details or payment_instrument object.

  • true: Don't reject the payment or verification for missing CVV alone. A CVV may still be present.
  • false or absent: Keep your existing CVV rules for that flow, including flows that accept payments without CVV.

Continue your fraud checks, 3-D Secure authentication, and validation of any CVV provided. The signal does not identify the originating vault. See the trusted vault origin reference for the field contract and payload examples.

Who's affected

This applies to payments apps that handle requests with payment_method.type set to credit_card. Your extension must use API version 2027-01 or later, and Shopify must enable the field for your app. Changing the API version does not enable it.

Shopify omits the field on earlier API versions, when it has not enabled the field for your app, or when it has no value to send.

What to do

No immediate production migration is required. Use the 2027-01 release candidate for testing and keep production apps on a supported stable version.

To prepare your integration:

  1. Review your payment and verification handlers. Add support for the optional field and the CVV handling described above.
  2. For integration testing, set your development extension's api_version to 2027-01. Confirm Shopify has enabled the field for your app before expecting Shopify to send it.
  3. Test true, false, and an absent field, with and without CVV. Cover each payload format your app supports and repeat the cases for verification requests if applicable. Confirm that missing CVV does not cause rejection for true, while false and absence preserve your existing handling.

title: Shop SDK lead capture now supports Rich Authorization Requests
summary:
You can now request the specific profile data your app needs during Shop SDK lead capture, including details that aren't saved on the user's Shop profile. Use Rich Authorization Requests (RAR) to select which fields are required and which ones users can skip. Existing integrations don't need changes to continue working; RAR is opt-in.

What changed

Lead capture now accepts an authorizationDetails attribute. The attribute takes a serialized JSON array that lists the fields your app needs and marks each one as required or optional. For example, this request requires a phone number and makes birthdate optional:

const authorizationDetails = JSON.stringify([
  {
    type: 'urn:shopify:shop_app:data-sharing:v1',
    datatypes: [
      {name: 'phone_number', required: true},
      {name: 'birthdate', required: false},
    ],
  },
]);

You can request given name, family name, phone number, and birthdate with RAR. The existing OAuth scopes shop_app:user:profile and shop_app:user:phone let you request existing names and phone numbers, respectively, but don't prompt users to provide missing values.

Before a user authorizes your app, Shop asks them for any requested fields that they haven't shared with your app. Users must provide values for required fields and can skip optional ones. If a user declines to authorize your app, then onComplete doesn't include a shopConsentToken, even if the user signs in to the store. Handle a missing shopConsentToken as an expected outcome.

Who's affected

This change applies to apps that use Shop SDK lead capture. To read data that you request with RAR, your app needs a client secret and a trusted server.

As with existing lead capture, an authorized phone number returned by Shop can replace a different phone number on the store's customer record. Existing names aren't replaced.

What to do

To request data with RAR:

  1. Pass your serialized array as attributes.authorizationDetails when you create the lead capture instance. To also request the user's identifier and email, set attributes.scope to 'shop_app:oauth', as shown in the guide.
  2. In onComplete, send shopConsentToken to your server when the event includes one. The event doesn't include the requested data. If the event includes customerUpdateErrors, then the update to the store's customer record failed.
  3. From your server, exchange the consent token with the fetchTokensForUser mutation on the Shop Partners API. Read the authorized fields from the response or from the Shop Users API, and handle null for fields that weren't granted or have no value.
  4. Before you ship, test a completed authorization, a skipped optional field, a declined authorization, and a request with malformed authorizationDetails JSON that returns invalid_authorization_details in onError. For the request format and error handling, see the lead capture guide.

Related docs

  • Lead capture
  • Get Shop user information

title: Shopify App Pricing: Plan Feature Targeting
summary:
You can now add store requirements to public plans in Shopify App Pricing. A merchant whose store does not have a required feature cannot subscribe to that plan. Store requirements are optional, so no action is required.

What changed

The plan editor in the Partner Dashboard has a new Store requirements section for public plans. You can select one or both of these requirements:

  • Checkout UI extensions (all pages) and branding customizations: The store can use app customizations on every step of checkout.
  • Direct company catalogs (B2B): The store can assign catalogs directly to its B2B customers.

Shopify checks the requirements on the plan selection page and again when the merchant approves the charge. On the plan selection page, the select button is unavailable on plans that the store does not qualify for.

Who's affected

Store requirements are available only on public plans in Shopify App Pricing. They are not available on private plans or on charges that you create with the Billing API. Requirements do not change existing subscriptions:

  • A merchant with an active subscription keeps the plan when you add or change its requirements.
  • If that subscription is cancelled, then the merchant must meet the current requirements to resume that plan.

Visitors who are not logged in to the Shopify App Store continue to see all of your public plans.

Why this matters

Before this change, a merchant could subscribe to a plan that depended on a feature their store did not have. Store requirements stop that subscription before the merchant pays for functionality that cannot work in their store.

What to do

No action is required. Add a store requirement only when a plan cannot work without the feature. Every store without the feature is blocked from the plan.

To add a store requirement:

  1. Open the plan editor for a public plan. For the full steps, refer to public plans.
  2. Under Store requirements, select the features that the plan needs.
  3. Click Save.
  4. Open your plan selection page from a store that does not have the feature.

The select button on that plan is unavailable, and the message names the missing feature. A store that has the feature can still select the plan.

  • Shopify App Pricing

title: Shopify App Store: Estimated local-currency prices
summary:
Merchants who are billed in a currency other than USD now see estimated prices for your app in their billing currency. No action is required on your part, and you can continue to set prices in USD.

What changed

The Shopify App Store and the Shopify admin show app prices as estimates in the merchant's billing currency, for example €17.67 EUR/month. Estimates appear in these places:

  • Your app listing and app cards on the Shopify App Store.
  • The plan selection page, the charge approval page, and app billing details in the Shopify admin.

A disclaimer next to each estimate shows the exchange rate. The disclaimer links to local currency billing in the Shopify Help Center.

Previously, these merchants saw USD prices and the message "All charges are billed in USD." Shopify still converts each charge to the merchant's billing currency when it issues the charge.

Who's affected

This change applies to apps that set prices in USD, with Shopify App Pricing or with the Billing API. Merchants see estimates when their billing currency is one of these 14 currencies: AUD, CAD, CHF, CZK, DKK, EUR, GBP, INR, JPY, NOK, PLN, RON, SEK, and SGD.

These cases do not change:

  • Merchants who are billed in USD see USD prices.
  • Charges that you create in another supported currency with the Billing API show their own amount.
  • Prices on app pages that you control are not converted.

What to do

No action is required. Your prices and earnings do not change. If your support content shows plan prices or screenshots, then check that it matches what merchants now see.

  • Estimated prices in local currencies
  • Shopify App Pricing

title: Introducing theme app add-ons: Build and bundle apps with your themes
summary:
Theme developers can now build storefront apps using theme app extensions and bundle them with their theme listings on the Theme Store. Theme app add-ons extend your theme with advanced functionality while creating new monetization opportunities through Shopify App Pricing.

Use theme app extensions to build app blocks that integrate natively with your theme, such as:

  • Product customization and configuration tools
  • Subscription and recurring purchase management
  • Advanced product filtering, search, and wishlists

Once your storefront app is published, you can add it to your theme in the Partner Dashboard.   • Apps can be listed or unlisted
  • The partner organization of the theme listing must own the app
  • One app add-on per theme; unlimited reuse across multiple themes

Theme developers building app add-ons will get priority in the app review queue, otherwise the usual review requirements still apply.

Resources

Learn more about building with theme app extensions and bundling apps with themes on shopify.dev.

title: Make your app's activity reportable in Shopify Analytics with App Events
summary:
You can now make your app’s activity available for merchants in Shopify Analytics. Merchants can explore your app’s metrics and dimensions in the report builder or query them with ShopifyQL using FROM app_events.

What changed

Apps can now declare events in an analytics_app_events extension. When an app sends a declared event through the App Events API, merchants can report on it in Shopify Analytics.

  • Use Shopify-defined standard events for common event types, such as emails sent.
  • Define custom events with attributes and metrics specific to your app.
  • Extend standard events with your own attributes and metrics.

Who's affected

This capability is available to developers who want merchants to report on activity from their installed apps in Shopify Analytics.

If your app already sends events for Dev Dashboard logs or billing, those events don’t automatically become available in Shopify Analytics. They must match a released Analytics App Events declaration. Existing App Events integrations don't need to change unless you want your events to appear in Shopify Analytics.

Why this matters

Merchants can now see your app's activity in Shopify Analytics, without leaving Shopify or opening a separate dashboard, and you don't need to build or host your own analytics. Your app shows up wherever merchants analyze their business.

What to do

No action is required unless you want to make app activity available in Shopify Analytics.

To get started, declare your standard or custom events in an analytics_app_events extension in shopify.extension.toml. For example, an email marketing app can declare the standard email-sent event: 

[[extensions]]
type = "analytics_app_events"
handle = "app-events"

[[extensions.events]]
name = "shopify.marketing.email_sent"
kind = "standard"

Release the configuration with shopify app deploy, then send matching events through the App Events API for stores where your app is installed.

Once the events are processed, merchants can report on emails sent over time using ShopifyQL:

FROM app_events
  SHOW emails_sent
  TIMESERIES day

Follow the App Events in Analytics guide to get started.

Related docs

  • App Events in Analytics
  • Configure Analytics App Events
  • Standard event registry
  • App Events API reference

title: App Events: Send events from Checkout and Customer Account UI extensions
summary:
Starting with API version 2027-01, Checkout and Customer Account UI extensions can send App Events to Shopify with shopify.appEvents.emit(). Extensions don't need network access or an app backend to send events. This is a new, optional API, so no action is required.

What changed

The new shopify.appEvents.emit() method sends a custom event with an event handle and optional attributes. Shopify adds your app and the shop to each event, so you don't need an access token or a shop ID. Events appear in your Dev Dashboard logs, together with the events that your app sends with the App Events API. For parameters, return values, and rate limits, refer to the API reference for Checkout UI extensions and Customer Account UI extensions.

Your extensions can also send the standard events that you declared for Shopify Analytics. Merchants see these events in their analytics.

Checkout and Customer Account send events only after the buyer allows analytics processing. Until then, events are held on the page. If the buyer declines or leaves the page, then the held events aren't sent.

Each extension can send a burst of 20 events, and then 2 events per second. When emit() doesn't send an event, it returns {success: false, error}. For example, this happens when the event is invalid or the extension exceeds the rate limit. Don't include personal information in event attributes.

Events from UI extensions aren't processed for billing. To report usage for Shopify App Pricing, continue to send billing events from your app's backend.

Who's affected

This change applies to Checkout UI extensions and Customer Account UI extensions that use API version 2027-01 or later. Extensions on earlier API versions don't have shopify.appEvents.

The server App Events API doesn't change, and apps without these extensions aren't affected. Checkouts in the Shop app don't send events from extensions.

Why this matters

Before this change, an extension needed network access and an app backend to send app events. Now an extension can send events directly, so you can see how buyers use your extension next to the rest of your app activity.

What to do

No action is required. To send events from an extension, follow these steps:

  1. Set api_version to 2027-01 in your extension's shopify.extension.toml file.
  2. Call shopify.appEvents.emit() where the event happens in your extension.
  3. In a development store, add the extension to checkout or customer account pages.
  4. If necessary, allow analytics processing as a buyer and make a test purchase. Confirm that the event appears in your Dev Dashboard logs. If you sent a declared standard event, then you can also find it in Analytics in your development store's Shopify admin.
shopify.appEvents.emit("offer_viewed", {
  offer_id: "summer_bundle",
  placement: "order_summary",
});

title: Shopify Flow: manage automations through AI Toolkit
summary:
You can now use an external agent to manage your Shopify Flow workflows through AI Toolkit. This release is for managing your own store's workflows via AI toolkit; third-party apps are prevented from using the underlying APIs directly.

What you can do:

Through AI Toolkit, you can ask your agent to manage automations in your shop:

  • Create, update, and delete workflows.
  • Activate and deactivate workflows.
  • Get a single or list of workflows.
  • Parse a .flow file into JSON that can be used with the API.
  • Get automation tasks and environment paths in order to build the workflow.

How to get started

You can use AI toolkit or the CLI to manage your automations. Using the new APIs directly require the write_automations scope, which is a Shopify approval scope and must be approved by Shopify.

AI toolkit

If you haven't previously used AI toolkit you should first get it working with your agent of choice.

If you previously used AI toolkit, the skill may be already available to you. If not you can ask your agent to update the shopify skill: 

Install or update the shopify skill from Shopify AI toolkit so that I can manage Flow automations

CLI

You can use the shopify store execute command to call the API directly.

API

To use the automation APIs directly, you must request the write_automations in a Shopify app. This scope must be approved by Shopify.

title: Managed mode for Shopify Tax
summary:
Shopify Tax managed mode helps Shopify apply the correct tax behavior for US sales by managing some store settings and API behavior directly. To keep those settings consistent, some Admin API writes now validate against the requirements of managed mode.

Managed mode sets requirements that Shopify uses to keep tax behavior consistent across a store. In some cases, the API now prevents apps from writing settings that would conflict with those requirements. In other cases, tax behavior now depends on more specific product or store data instead of simple boolean settings.

For app developers, the main pattern is:

  • Requests that already use the required settings, or that omit settings the app doesn't need to manage, continue to work.
  • Requests that try to override managed-mode requirements might now return validation errors.

These changes affect apps that configure markets, publish products, create custom line items, or preview checkout branding for stores that use Shopify Tax managed mode. The changes fall into four categories:

  • Breaking changes: Markets API writes and product publishing writes can now fail when they conflict with Shopify Tax managed mode requirements.
  • Deprecation: The taxable input on custom line items is deprecated in favor of productCategoryId.
  • New capability: Apps can assign product categories to custom line items in draft orders and order edits.
  • Behavior clarification: Checkout footer visibility controls merchant-configurable content only, not Shopify-provided transaction information.

Breaking: Markets API writes require fixed US defaults

For stores that use Shopify Tax in managed mode for US sales, the marketCreate and marketUpdate mutations now reject attempts to override required currency and tax-display defaults for affected markets. The validation applies only to merchant-managed, non-retail markets that include the United States. Markets without the United States, retail markets, and third-party-managed markets are excluded.

Stores that don't use Shopify Tax managed mode are unaffected even if they sell to US customers.

Affected requests

This change applies across all supported API versions, including unstable. The validation only applies when a request supplies currencySettings or priceInclusions, so requests that omit these inputs are unchanged. When one of these inputs is submitted, Shopify validates the resulting setting, including retained values and defaults for omitted subfields.

If your app sets these fields, use the required defaults or omit fields that your app doesn't need to manage.

For a US-only market, the following optional inputs use the required defaults:

{
  "currencySettings": {
    "baseCurrency": "USD",
    "localCurrencies": false
  },
  "priceInclusions": {
    "taxPricingStrategy": "ADD_TAXES_AT_CHECKOUT"
  }
}

For a market that includes the United States and another country, such as Canada, the following optional inputs use the required defaults:

{
  "currencySettings": {
    "localCurrencies": true
  },
  "priceInclusions": {
    "taxPricingStrategy": "INCLUDES_TAXES_IN_PRICE_BASED_ON_COUNTRY"
  }
}

Handle validation errors through userErrors.code, userErrors.field, and userErrors.message. Currency violations return UNSUPPORTED_CURRENCY. Tax-display violations return INCOMPATIBLE_CONFIGURATION on API version 2026-07 and later, or GENERIC_ERROR on earlier versions.

Breaking: Product publishing requires the Shop channel

For stores that use Shopify Tax managed mode, products published to Online Store, Headless, Hydrogen, or Buy Button must also be published to Shop. These channels depend on Shop, so requests that would leave a product on one of these channels without Shop are handled differently by API version. In unstable, the request fails. In dated versions, Shopify adds the missing Shop or dependent-channel changes to the request and saves it. Shopify doesn't save any part of a failed request.

The failures described below apply to the unstable API version. Dated versions apply the same rules, but change the request instead of failing it. Refer to Dated API versions. Stores that don't use Shopify Tax managed mode are unaffected, and requests that only change other sales channels, collections, or product variants are unchanged. The change is rolling out gradually to stores that use managed mode, with no schema changes.

Affected requests

A product counts as being on a channel when it's published there, scheduled to publish there, or, for draft products, added to that channel. A request that includes both Shop and a dependent channel is checked as a whole, in any order.

The validation applies to publishablePublish, publishableUnpublish, and publicationUpdate. It also applies to deprecated GraphQL publishing APIs, including productPublish, productUnpublish, and the publishing fields on productCreate and productUpdate. For the REST Admin API, product create and update requests fail when they would put a product on Online Store while the product isn't on Shop or is blocked by Shop.

Additional validation rules apply:

  • Shop blocks a product when it rejects the product or flags it as needing action. publishablePublish fails if Shop blocks the product and the resulting state leaves it on a dependent channel, even if the request publishes only to Shop. productUpdate also fails if Shop blocks the product and the resulting state leaves it on a dependent channel.

  • Removing a product from Shop requires removing its dependent-channel publications, in any state. This applies to publishableUnpublish and to publicationUpdate removals from Shop.

  • For publicationUpdate:

    • Adding a product to a dependent channel fails if the product isn’t on Shop or Shop blocks it. Adding a blocked product to Shop also fails if it remains on a dependent channel. Products already in the target publication aren’t checked when included in publishablesToAdd.
    • publicationUpdate rejects autoPublish: true on a dependent channel when Shop’s publication doesn’t auto-publish. It also rejects autoPublish: false on Shop when a dependent channel still auto-publishes.

  • On productUpdate, publications replace the product’s entire publication list. Include Shop whenever the replacement list includes a dependent channel, even if the product is already on Shop. When the request also changes status, validation uses the new status.

The deprecated productPublish and productUnpublish mutations follow the same failure conditions as publishablePublish and publishableUnpublish.

Dated API versions

On dated API versions, Shopify changes a request that breaks these rules so that it follows them, then saves it:

  • Publishing a product to a dependent channel also publishes it to Shop. Shop doesn't support scheduled publishing, so Shopify publishes to Shop immediately, even when the dependent channel is scheduled.
  • Removing a product from Shop also removes it from its dependent channels.
  • On productCreate and productUpdate, including the product-level publishing fields, Shop is added when the request puts the product on Online Store or another dependent channel. On productUpdate, a publications list that leaves out Shop keeps the product on Shop.
  • For publicationUpdate, adding products to a dependent channel also adds them to Shop, and removing products from Shop also removes them from dependent channels. Turning on autoPublish for a dependent channel also turns it on for Shop. Turning off autoPublish for Shop also turns it off for dependent channels.
  • A Shop rejection or a "needs action" flag doesn't block the request.
  • REST Admin API product, product listing, and product publication requests behave the same way.

If the request still breaks the rules after these changes, it fails with the same error as in unstable. For example, this happens when a draft product is scheduled on a dependent channel without Shop.

Keep in mind:

  • If your app publishes products to Online Store, Headless, Hydrogen, or Buy Button, publish the product to Shop first or include Shop in the same request. If your app unpublishes a product from Shop, unpublish it from dependent channels first or include those removals in the same request.
  • If your app creates active products with the REST Admin API, send "published": false, then publish the product to Shop and Online Store with publishablePublish.
  • On dated versions, Shopify can publish a product to Shop, or remove it from dependent channels, even when your request didn't name those channels. To control the result, send Shop and its dependent channels together.

Handle these failures as validation errors. Retrying the same request returns the same error. Publishing requests fail with For the store setup, Shop publication is a prerequisite. Unpublishing requests fail with For the store setup, unpublishing from dependent publications is a prerequisite.

Deprecated: taxable on custom line items

The taxable input for custom line items in draft orders and order edits is deprecated in favor of productCategoryId, which assigns a category from Shopify's Standard Product Taxonomy and lets Shopify determine the item's tax treatment.

On GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01 and later, DraftOrderLineItemInput.taxable and the taxable argument on orderEditAddCustomItem are marked as deprecated. Apps on API version 2026-10 or earlier don't see a schema change.

  • Reading the taxable state isn't deprecated, so fields that return whether a line item is taxable, and webhook payloads that include taxable state, are unchanged.
  • For stores using Shopify Tax managed mode, taxable is ignored on custom line items in every API version. The product category sets tax treatment, and a custom line item with no category is taxed at the standard rate. For all other stores, taxable works as before.

If your app sets taxable when creating or editing custom line items, replace it with productCategoryId on GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01 or later. To exempt an entire draft order on a store that uses Shopify Tax managed mode, mark the customer, company, or company location as tax-exempt. Use a category to exempt a single item.

New: Set product categories on custom line items in draft orders and order edits

You can now assign a category from Shopify's Standard Product Taxonomy to custom line items in draft orders and order edits. The category controls the item's tax treatment in the same way it does for products.

For stores using Shopify Tax managed mode, productCategoryId is the input that sets a custom line item's tax treatment. The taxable input is ignored. A custom line item with no category is treated as Uncategorized and taxed at the standard rate.

For stores that don't use Shopify Tax managed mode, taxable: false continues to mean that the custom line item isn't taxed. When the item is taxed, Shopify can use its category to calculate tax.

Affected requests

In draft orders, DraftOrderLineItemInput.productCategoryId sets the product category for a custom line item in draftOrderCreate, draftOrderUpdate, and draftOrderCalculate. It's ignored when variantId is provided. You can read the saved category from DraftOrderLineItem.productCategory and CalculatedDraftOrderLineItem.productCategory; these fields return null for product variant line items.

In order edits, orderEditAddCustomItem accepts a new productCategoryId argument. You can read the category from CalculatedLineItem.productCategory.

If productCategoryId doesn't match a category in the current taxonomy, the mutation returns a user error.

A product category can express reduced rates, exemptions, and category-specific tax rules that a yes-or-no taxable value can't. To use it, look up a category ID with the taxonomy query, pass the ID as productCategoryId, and read the saved category from the relevant productCategory field.

query {
  taxonomy {
    categories(search: "t-shirts", first: 5) {
      nodes {
        id
        fullName
      }
    }
  }
}

Clarification: Checkout footer visibility controls merchant-configurable content only

The visibility fields on CheckoutBrandingFooterContent and CheckoutAndAccountsConfigurationBrandingFooterContent now control only merchant-configurable footer content. All checkout and Thank you pages can display the additional Shopify-provided transaction information in the footer when visibility is set to HIDDEN.

Merchant-configurable footer content includes merchant policy links and copyright copy. Shopify-provided transaction information is part of checkout, isn't controlled by checkout branding, and isn't configurable through these visibility settings.

This affects apps that customize checkout branding for Shopify Plus stores through the legacy Checkout Branding API or the Checkout and Accounts Configuration API, especially apps that manage footer visibility, render branding previews, or run visual tests. Apps that don't manage checkout footer visibility are unaffected.

No fields, input types, enum values, access scopes, or mutations have changed. The clarification applies to every GraphQL Admin API version where the corresponding branding type exists; it isn't tied to a new API version.

Existing mutations and stored branding configurations continue to work without changes. If your app previews or tests checkout branding, update it so Shopify-provided transaction information can remain visible when merchant-configurable footer content is hidden.

    }

The visibility fields on CheckoutBrandingFooterContent and CheckoutAndAccountsConfigurationBrandingFooterContent now control only merchant-configurable footer content. title: First sign-ins to customer accounts now set Customer.state and send customers/enable webhooks
summary:
A customer's first sign-in to customer accounts now sets Customer.state to ENABLED and sends the customers/enable and customers/update webhooks. This matches how account activation works in legacy customer accounts.

What's changing

When a customer signs in to customer accounts for the first time, Shopify sets Customer.state to ENABLED. Shopify then sends the customers/enable and customers/update webhooks. This happens for every sign-in method, including email code, Shop, Google, Facebook, Apple, and third-party identity providers.

Until now, customers who used customer accounts stayed DISABLED after they signed in. As a result, Liquid customer.has_account returned false for them. It now returns true after their first sign-in.

Customers who already signed in

Customers who signed in to customer accounts between May 27, 2024 and today are already ENABLED. Shopify set their state in a one-time update that didn't send any webhooks. Don't rely on updated_at to find these customers, because the update didn't change it for all of them. Query Customer.state instead.

Customers who haven't signed in since May 27, 2024 stay DISABLED. Their next sign-in counts as a first sign-in. It sets their state to ENABLED and sends both webhooks.

Who's affected

You're affected if your app, integration, or theme does any of the following:

  • Reads Customer.state from the GraphQL Admin API
  • Listens for the customers/enable or customers/update webhooks
  • Consumes customer.state events from the Events API
  • Uses Liquid customer.has_account to check whether a customer has an account

What you should do

Most apps don't need changes. If your app sends welcome messages, awards loyalty points, or syncs records when it receives customers/enable or sees state: ENABLED, check these things:

  • A customer's first sign-in is the moment you want your app to act.
  • Your app handles customers who became ENABLED in the one-time update. They didn't trigger webhooks, so an app that only listens for webhooks won't see them.
  • Your theme still works as you expect now that customer.has_account returns true for customers who signed in to customer accounts.

title: Add selling plans to draft order line items with the Admin GraphQL API
summary:
Admin GraphQL API version 2027-01 adds selling plan support to draft orders. You can now apply a selling plan to a draft order line item and read back the applied plan. These fields are additive, so no action is required to keep your app working.

What's added

On the GraphQL Admin API, three new fields let your app work with selling plans on draft orders:

  • DraftOrderLineItemInput.sellingPlanId sets the selling plan to apply when you create or update a draft order line item. This input field can apply to draftOrderCalculate, draftOrderCreate, and draftOrderUpdate. Note that you can only attach selling plans to product variant line items.
  • DraftOrderLineItem.sellingPlanApplication returns the selling plan applied to a line item on a saved draft order.
  • CalculatedDraftOrderLineItem.sellingPlanApplication returns the applied selling plan on the calculated draft order, so you can preview the result before you save.

The following example applies a selling plan to a line item and reads back the applied plan:

mutation {
  draftOrderCreate(input: {
    lineItems: [{
      variantId: "gid://shopify/ProductVariant/1",
      quantity: 1,
      sellingPlanId: "gid://shopify/SellingPlan/1"
    }]
  }) {
    draftOrder {
      lineItems(first: 1) {
        nodes {
          sellingPlanApplication { sellingPlanId name }
        }
      }
    }
    userErrors { field message }
  }
}

Behavior to account for

  • Only recurring and prepaid subscription plans are supported. Fixed-billing plans, such as pre-orders and try before you buy, aren't.
  • B2B draft orders, custom line items, and price overrides on selling plan lines aren't supported.
  • draftOrderComplete is not yet supported: calling draftOrderComplete on a draft that has a selling plan line item returns a user error and creates no order. You can send the draft order invoice to checkout via draftOrderInvoiceSend.

Learn more about this change in our product changelog and help docs.

title: Cart and checkout permalinks now support UCP at /buy
summary:
Shopify storefronts now support the UCP dev.ucp.shopping.permalink capability starting with UCP 2026-08-25 on a new /buy route. You can use a single /buy link to add items to a cart, prefill checkout details, and take the buyer to checkout, using the same link format on any shop that supports UCP. You don’t need to change existing integrations to keep them working.

What changed

Shops now list the dev.ucp.shopping.permalink capability in their UCP discovery profile at /.well-known/ucp, and its config.endpoint points to the shop’s /buy route.

A /buy link encodes items in the path as token:quantity pairs and sets other cart and checkout fields with query parameters named by their UCP field path, such as buyer/email or discounts/codes/0.

With a /buy link, you can:

  • Add one or more items by variant ID
  • Prefill buyer details, such as email address
  • Set the buyer’s country and language
  • Apply discount codes
  • Indicate a preference for Shop Pay
  • Send the buyer to a specific page on the shop with a continue_to parameter

If a link can’t be applied, Shopify redirects the buyer to the continue_to destination when it’s present, or to the shop’s storefront instead of showing an error page.

Existing /cart permalinks keep working, although they’re now the legacy format. Shopify keeps supporting them, but new capabilities go to /buy. /buy doesn’t support selling plans, line item properties, cart notes, or cart attributes yet, so you should keep using /cart if you need those features.

What to do

Use /buy for new links, and move existing /cart links to /buy where you can. New capabilities only apply to /buy, and the same link format works on any business that supports UCP. Your /cart links keep working, so you can migrate on your own schedule. If you rely on selling plans, line item properties, cart notes, or cart attributes, keep using /cart for now.

Permalinks don’t use capability negotiation, so you don’t need to declare dev.ucp.shopping.permalink in your agent profile. To build a link, read config.endpoint from the shop’s discovery profile instead of constructing the /buy URL yourself.

Never put payment credentials or access tokens in a link, and avoid buyer personal details in links you share widely.

title: Store and app install details in the Dev Dashboard
summary:
You can now view your organization’s installed apps, collaborator access, earnings, and app activity in one place in the Dev Dashboard.

Use the store page to view apps, users, and earnings for a store:

  • Apps from your organization installed on the store.
  • Users in your organization who have collaborator access to the store.
  • Earnings from the store, including total app earnings, total theme earnings, and recurring revenue share.

You can also dig in by app, with app install details:

  • Gross lifetime earnings from that store for the selected app.
  • An activity feed of installation and billing events.
  • The app’s current subscription, with quick access to logs for that store.

To get started, select a store in Stores in the Dev Dashboard. For app install details, open your app’s Overview, select the install count in the Installs card, then select a store. Available details depend on your permissions and store access.

Learn more about store details and app install details, including available information and permissions.

title: Manage payouts, billing, and settings in Dev Dashboard
summary:
You now manage your Partner business details, payouts, billing, and the remaining Partner Dashboard settings in Dev Dashboard's Organization settings. New Partners also complete business verification there during setup. Existing Partners don’t need to take action because your current payout and billing settings stay the same.

What changed

The Settings and Payouts links in Partner Dashboard and the Home payout widget have moved to Dev Dashboard. To reach the new pages, open Dev Dashboard, select your organization, and open Organization settings.

From Organization settings, you can manage:

  • Organization details: business and contact details, emergency contact, App Store registration, and Partner ID
  • Payouts: payout setup, history, transactions, and payout methods
  • Partner billing: bills, ad invoices, payment methods, invoice notes, and ad credits
  • Users > Security: Partner API clients

What to do

Your payout or billing settings are migrated over, and no action is required.

To learn more about where Partner Dashboard features have moved in Dev Dashboard, see the migration guide. For more about Dev Dashboard in general, see the Overview.
